info.text: Interactive check questions for Lesson 12.1: Drafting Scholarly Commentary Notes by Hand: Categories, Anchors, and TEI Encoding.

name.text: 01 Question: The Purpose of Scholarly Commentary

questiontext.text: Why is scholarly commentary essential when publishing historical archival documents?

generalfeedback.text: Scholarly commentary is an active editorial practice that provides the historical, linguistic, and cultural context readers need to understand primary documents.

answer.text: It provides the historical, linguistic, and cultural context readers need to understand primary documents across time and distance.

feedback.text: Correct. Commentary acts as an intentional interpretive bridge explaining archaic vocabulary, historical figures, and obsolete legal concepts.

answer.text: It serves exclusively to fix typographical printing errors made by modern publishers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Correcting printer typos is proofreading, not scholarly commentary.

answer.text: It replaces the original historical wording with an uncritical modern paraphrase.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Commentary engages and explicates the primary witness rather than replacing it.

answer.text: It acts purely as decorative ornament without making any substantive analytical claims.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Commentary is an active research genre that mediates meaning for readers.

name.text: 02 Question: The Editorial Layers of a Digital Edition

questiontext.text: How does scholarly commentary differ methodologically from diplomatic transcription and normalization?

generalfeedback.text: Commentary provides the interpretive rationale behind textual features, remaining distinct from physical text record and linguistic normalization.

answer.text: Transcription records raw characters and normalization standardizes spelling, while commentary explains historical meaning and cultural significance.

feedback.text: Correct. Each layer serves a distinct purpose: transcription captures physical ink strokes, normalization aligns spelling, and commentary unpacks interpretive meaning.

answer.text: Transcription translates foreign words, normalization marks line breaks, and commentary records raw ink strokes.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This inverts the editorial layers.

answer.text: Commentary is only used for ancient Greek texts, while transcription is used for modern English letters.

feedback.text: Incorrect. All digital editions combine transcription, normalization, and commentary regardless of language.

answer.text: Commentary collapses all editorial notes into an undifferentiated footnote to save digital space.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Digital editions separate notes into structured analytical categories rather than collapsing them.

name.text: 03 Question: The Three Core Categories of Commentary Notes

questiontext.text: Which three core categories structure digital commentary notes to ensure consistent annotation and automated indexing?

generalfeedback.text: Grouping commentary into language, historical, and intertextual categories ensures consistent annotation and enables automated indexing.

answer.text: Philological/Lexical, Historical/Contextual, and Intertextual/Citational.

feedback.text: Correct. These three domains cover words and grammar, real-world context and people, and connections to external documents.

answer.text: Diplomatic, Paleographical, and Codicological.

feedback.text: Incorrect. These describe physical manuscript features, not the domains of scholarly commentary.

answer.text: Introductory, Intermediate, and Advanced.

feedback.text: Incorrect. These describe pedagogical difficulty levels, not commentary categories.

answer.text: Font, Margin, and Color.

feedback.text: Incorrect. These are visual styling attributes, not scholarly annotation categories.

name.text: 04 Question: Category 1: language and Lexical Notes

questiontext.text: In Andromeda's 1752 Peace and Friendship Treaty, what does a philological note clarify regarding the term 'Truckhouse'?

generalfeedback.text: language notes clarify obsolete vocabulary, historical legal terminology, and regional expressions to prevent modern misinterpretation.

answer.text: It defines 'Truckhouse' as an 18th-century government-run trading post where Mi'kmaq hunters exchanged furs for goods at regulated rates.

feedback.text: Correct. Philological notes clarify obsolete or specialized historical vocabulary that modern readers might otherwise misunderstand.

answer.text: It explains that 'Truckhouse' was a mechanical automobile repair garage in colonial Halifax.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Motorized vehicles did not exist in 1752; the term refers to a commercial trading post.

answer.text: It proves that the word was a scribal spelling error that should be deleted from the treaty text.

feedback.text: Incorrect. 'Truckhouse' was standard 18th-century colonial terminology for a trade depot.

answer.text: It translates the word into modern classical Latin.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The note explains historical English usage rather than translating into Latin.

name.text: 05 Question: Category 2: Historical and Contextual Notes

questiontext.text: What is the primary function of a historical and contextual commentary note?

generalfeedback.text: Historical notes identify people, places, dates, and institutions, giving readers the essential background context behind the text.

answer.text: To identify people, places, dates, and institutions, providing essential background context for the document.

feedback.text: Correct. Historical notes identify real-world entities like Governor Peregrine Hopson, Marshalltown, or the French National Assembly.

answer.text: To parse the grammatical gender and case ending of every noun in the sentence.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Grammatical parsing is the role of linguistic and philological notes.

answer.text: To copy an entire multi-page encyclopedia entry into the margin of the digital edition.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Effective historical notes are concise and focused directly on the passage.

answer.text: To predict future political events that took place centuries after the document was created.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Historical notes explain the contemporary historical context of the document.

name.text: 06 Question: Category 3: Intertextual and Citational Notes

questiontext.text: In Ace's 1791 French Revolutionary decree, why is an intertextual commentary note necessary when previous financial legislation is mentioned?

generalfeedback.text: Intertextual notes identify and explain citations, legal cross-references, and literary echoes that link a document to a wider network of texts.

answer.text: It identifies the specific decree of September 1790 being referenced, linking readers to the earlier law and its legal precedents.

feedback.text: Correct. Intertextual notes uncover the network of legal codes, previous treaties, and correspondence cited by the primary witness.

answer.text: It translates the French text into rhyming English poetry.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Intertextual notes document citations and textual relations, not poetic translations.

answer.text: It deletes the citation because historical laws are irrelevant to modern digital editions.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Tracking legal cross-references is essential for understanding historical legislation.

answer.text: It records the name of the modern printer who scanned the PDF document.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Intertextual notes trace historical and legal connections, not modern scan technician metadata.

name.text: 07 Question: The Dilemma of Text Anchors

questiontext.text: Why do modern digital editions avoid using raw character offsets to connect commentary notes to text passages?

generalfeedback.text: Robust digital commentary relies on stable XML identifier anchors rather than fragile character offsets that break when text is revised.

answer.text: Raw character offsets break whenever text is edited or typos are corrected earlier in the file, whereas XML identifiers remain completely stable.

feedback.text: Correct. Assigning unique xml:id attributes creates permanent anchors that survive subsequent edits and corrections.

answer.text: Character offsets take up too much memory for modern web browsers to process.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Character offsets are computationally trivial, but conceptually fragile when files are edited.

answer.text: Character offsets are forbidden by international copyright law.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Copyright law does not govern internal XML anchor indexing mechanisms.

answer.text: XML parsers cannot count numbers higher than 256.

feedback.text: Incorrect. XML parsers handle arbitrary numbers without issue.

name.text: 08 Question: scope of Anchors: Words, Spans, and Sentences

questiontext.text: Which anchor granularity is best suited for explaining the historical background of a treaty clause or revolutionary article?

generalfeedback.text: Match your anchor scope to the purpose of the note: use word anchors for lexical glosses, and sentence or phrase anchors for historical commentary.

answer.text: A sentence or clause anchor (<s xml:id='...'>), which encompasses the full conceptual statement.

feedback.text: Correct. Sentence anchors provide a clean target for thematic and legal commentary without cluttering individual words.

answer.text: A single punctuation mark anchor (<pc xml:id='...'>).

feedback.text: Incorrect. Punctuation anchors are too narrow to anchor broad historical commentary.

answer.text: An entire 500-page book archive without any internal subdivisions.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Whole-book anchors are far too vague for readers to locate the annotated passage.

answer.text: A raw pixel coordinate on the computer monitor screen.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Pixel coordinates break across different screen resolutions and layout modes.

name.text: 09 Question: The Problem of Overlapping Markup

questiontext.text: Why can traditional inline <note> tags cause fatal XML syntax errors when annotating multi-line or multi-sentence passages?

generalfeedback.text: XML requires strict tree nesting, making it impossible to overlap inline tags across element boundaries.

answer.text: XML enforces strict tree nesting, making it syntactically invalid to close a parent tag before closing an embedded note tag.

feedback.text: Correct. Tags that overlap across structural boundaries (such as lines and sentences) violate XML well-formedness rules.

answer.text: XML forbids the letter 'n' from appearing inside angle brackets.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Element names routinely include 'n', such as <note> and <name>.

answer.text: Inline notes cause computer monitors to overheat when rendering long sentences.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Overlapping markup is a syntactic parser violation, not a hardware issue.

answer.text: Browsers automatically delete any text enclosed in an inline note.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Browsers render inline notes unless hidden by CSS, but malformed XML halts parser execution entirely.

name.text: 10 Question: Introduction to TEI Standoff Markup

questiontext.text: How does TEI standoff markup solve the overlapping hierarchy problem in digital editions?

generalfeedback.text: Standoff markup places annotations in a separate `` section, keeping base text clean and allowing complex, multi-point linking.

answer.text: It isolates commentary notes in a separate <standOff> container, linking them back to text anchors via URI pointers without embedding tags inside the text.

feedback.text: Correct. Standoff markup keeps the base transcription clean and allows notes to point to multiple discontinuous anchors without breaking XML tree rules.

answer.text: It converts all XML tags into plain unformatted ASCII text files.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Standoff markup is standard, fully valid TEI XML.

answer.text: It deletes the original transcription and replaces it with commentary notes only.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The base transcription remains intact in the <body>.

answer.text: It requires students to write their notes on physical paper note cards rather than computers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Standoff markup is a digital encoding architecture inside the XML file.

name.text: 11 Question: TEI Chapter 17: Simple Analytic Mechanisms

questiontext.text: What standardized elements does TEI Chapter 17 provide for encoding qualitative thematic interpretations?

generalfeedback.text: TEI Chapter 17 provides standardized elements (``, ``, and ``) for encoding structured interpretive metadata.

answer.text: <interpGrp> and <interp>, which define controlled thematic categories and link them to text spans.

feedback.text: Correct. Chapter 17 provides simple analytic mechanisms for structured qualitative tagging and thematic analysis.

answer.text: <html> and <body>, which format web page headings.

feedback.text: Incorrect. These are HTML layout tags, not TEI Chapter 17 analytical elements.

answer.text: <graphic> and <surface>, which record digital image coordinates.

feedback.text: Incorrect. These belong to TEI Chapter 11 (Facsimiles), not Chapter 17.

answer.text: <app> and <rdg>, which record textual variants in an apparatus criticus.

feedback.text: Incorrect. These belong to TEI Chapter 12 (Critical Apparatus).

name.text: 12 Question: Encoding Controlled Interpretations with <interpGrp>

questiontext.text: How does defining treaty themes in an <interpGrp> enhance searchability in Andromeda's 1752 Treaty edition?

generalfeedback.text: Defining themes in an `` sets up a controlled vocabulary that makes commentary themes systematically searchable across an entire edition.

answer.text: It establishes a controlled vocabulary (e.g., trade regulations, peace terms) so software can query all passages sharing a specific theme via the @ana attribute.

feedback.text: Correct. Controlled vocabularies prevent spelling drift and allow faceted thematic filtering across the entire document.

answer.text: It automatically translates the English treaty into every modern European language.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Controlled thematic vocabularies enable search and categorization, not automated translation.

answer.text: It prevents unauthorized readers from accessing the digital edition.

feedback.text: Incorrect. <interpGrp> is an analytical metadata tool, not a security encryption system.

answer.text: It forces all sentences in the treaty to be exactly the same character length.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Thematic grouping has no effect on sentence length.

name.text: 13 Question: Pointing and Linking: The Syntax of @target

questiontext.text: When linking a standoff <note> to an anchor with xml:id='s12' in the same document, what is the mandatory syntax for @target?

generalfeedback.text: The `@target` attribute links standoff notes to text anchors using the `#id` syntax, supporting multiple space-separated targets.

answer.text: target='#s12', including the required hash symbol (#) prefix to denote an internal fragment identifier.

feedback.text: Correct. The hash symbol (#) is mandatory; omitting it causes the processor to look for an external file named 's12' rather than an internal ID.

answer.text: target='s12', without any punctuation marks.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Omitting the hash prefix is a syntax error for local fragment pointers.

answer.text: target='@s12', using an at-sign symbol.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The at-sign denotes an XML attribute in XPath, not a URI fragment identifier.

answer.text: target='*s12', using an asterisk.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Asterisks are not valid URI fragment markers in TEI.

name.text: 14 Question: standard Inline <note> vs. Standoff <note>

questiontext.text: When is it appropriate to use an inline <note> rather than a standoff note in a scholarly edition?

generalfeedback.text: Use inline notes only for original author footnotes found in the source. Use standoff notes for modern scholarly commentary.

answer.text: When recording an original footnote or authorial marginal note physically printed or written in the primary witness.

feedback.text: Correct. Inline notes represent authorial or scribal notes that belong to the physical document itself, whereas modern editorial commentary belongs in standoff markup.

answer.text: When writing a modern 500-word essay about 18th-century French politics.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Long modern essays should be placed in standoff containers or introductory appendices to prevent cluttering the text.

answer.text: Whenever the editor wants to hide text so that students cannot read it.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Inline notes are not an access restriction tool.

answer.text: Only when the document is written in French.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Markup architecture choices depend on the editorial function of the note, not the language of the source text.

name.text: 15 Question: Typing Commentary Notes with @type and @subtype

questiontext.text: Why should digital editors enrich <note> elements with @type and @subtype attributes?

generalfeedback.text: Classify every commentary note using `@type` and `@subtype` so digital editions can filter annotations by analytical domain.

answer.text: To allow reading interfaces and search tools to filter notes by domain (e.g., showing only historical notes or only linguistic glosses).

feedback.text: Correct. Typed notes enable faceted filtering so readers can focus on their specific research interests without distraction.

answer.text: To change the background color of the computer monitor automatically.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Semantic attributes describe analytical meaning, not hardware display colors.

answer.text: Because untyped notes cause XML validators to delete the file permanently.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Untyped notes are valid XML, but lack semantic precision.

answer.text: To prevent search engines from finding the notes online.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Typed notes improve search engine discovery and linked open data indexing.

name.text: 16 Question: Structuring Rich Note Bodies

questiontext.text: Which TEI element should be used inside a commentary note to identify a specific word from the base text that is being discussed?

generalfeedback.text: Structure the interior of commentary notes using ``, ``, and `` to maintain academic rigor and book attribution.

answer.text: <mentioned>

feedback.text: Correct. The <mentioned> element marks a word or phrase from the base text being cited or analyzed within a note.

answer.text: <delete>

feedback.text: Incorrect. <delete> is not a standard TEI element for word discussion; <del> marks editorial deletions in transcription.

answer.text: <foreign>

feedback.text: Incorrect. <foreign> marks words in another language, whereas <mentioned> marks a term being discussed regardless of language.

answer.text: <code>

feedback.text: Incorrect. <code> is an HTML tag for programming code, not a TEI linguistic analysis tag.

name.text: 17 Question: Attributing Editorial credit with @resp

questiontext.text: In a collaborative digital edition, how does the @resp attribute ensure scholarly transparency and accountability?

generalfeedback.text: Attribute every commentary note to its human author or AI assistant using `@resp` to maintain scholarly clarity and honesty.

answer.text: It links each note to a declared editor or AI model in the teiHeader (e.g., resp='#al' or resp='#gemini'), making authorship explicit.

feedback.text: Correct. The @resp pointer credits human student editors and transparently identifies machine-generated draft suggestions.

answer.text: It hides student names to protect them from public academic scrutiny.

feedback.text: Incorrect. @resp provides transparent attribution, not anonymization.

answer.text: It automatically grades the student's assignment based on the number of notes written.

feedback.text: Incorrect. @resp is a metadata attribution tool, not an automated grading script.

answer.text: It sends an automated email to the university registrar whenever a note is saved.

feedback.text: Incorrect. XML attributes record metadata within the document without triggering email alerts.

name.text: 18 Question: Connecting Commentary to External standard Files

questiontext.text: How does adding an external URI via the @ref attribute (such as a Wikidata or GeoNames link) benefit a digital edition?

generalfeedback.text: Enrich commentary notes with standard URIs (`@ref`) to link your local edition to the global web of historical and geographical data.

answer.text: It connects local document notes to global Linked Open Data networks, providing persistent identifiers and disambiguating historical entities.

feedback.text: Correct. Linking to Wikidata or GeoNames ensures that 'Digby' or 'Louis XVI' resolves to globally standardized authority records.

answer.text: It forces readers to pay an annual subscription fee to access the external website.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Wikidata and GeoNames are open-access public resources.

answer.text: It replaces the primary text with satellite photographs of modern cities.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Authority links provide external reference data without altering the primary text.

answer.text: It automatically translates the document into computer binary machine code.

feedback.text: Incorrect. URI links provide web addresses, not binary machine code translation.

name.text: 19 Question: Step-by-Step: Preparing Your Document for Annotation in VS Code

questiontext.text: What is the first technical step you must perform in VS Code before writing standoff commentary notes?

generalfeedback.text: Prepare your document in VS Code by verifying XML well-formedness, setting sequential `xml:id` anchors, and setting up a two-column editor layout.

answer.text: Verify that your base text is well-formed XML and ensure target sentences or words carry unique xml:id attributes.

feedback.text: Correct. Standoff notes require stable xml:id anchors; verifying well-formedness ensures pointers will resolve cleanly.

answer.text: Delete all XML tags and convert the document into a Microsoft Word file.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI scholarly editions are maintained in XML, not converted to Word.

answer.text: Change all text font colors to bright red.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Visual styling is handled by CSS, not preparatory XML editing.

answer.text: Turn off the internet connection to prevent VS Code from updating.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Internet connectivity does not interfere with local XML anchor preparation.

name.text: 20 Question: Hands-On Walkthrough: Drafting language Notes

questiontext.text: When drafting a philological note on Maud Lewis's colloquial use of the word 'crooked' to describe her hands, what should the note explain?

generalfeedback.text: Author language notes by naming specialized terms, researching their historical definitions, and linking them to word or sentence anchors via `@target`.

answer.text: It should explain that Lewis used the word to describe physical joint deformities caused by juvenile rheumatoid arthritis, citing medical and biographical sources.

feedback.text: Correct. Philological notes clarify colloquial or non-standard usage with verified historical and biographical context.

answer.text: It should claim that Maud Lewis was dishonest and crooked in her business dealings.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Lewis was referring to her physical hands, not her moral character.

answer.text: It should replace the word 'crooked' with modern medical terminology directly in the primary text.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Editorial commentary explains historical terms without tampering with primary witness text.

answer.text: It should state that the word has no known meaning in the English language.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The colloquial usage is well documented in Maritime folk speech and Lewis scholarship.

name.text: 21 Question: Hands-On Walkthrough: Drafting Historical Notes

questiontext.text: What essential information should be included in a historical commentary note identifying Mi'kmaq Chief Jean-Baptiste Cope in the 1752 Treaty?

generalfeedback.text: Historical notes explain persons and institutions by synthesizing verified biographical facts and linking them to external biographical dictionaries.

answer.text: His historical leadership role in the Shubenacadie district, his diplomatic objectives in negotiating the treaty, and verified biographical dates.

feedback.text: Correct. Historical notes synthesize verified biographical and institutional context directly relevant to the document.

answer.text: A full transcript of modern 21st-century Canadian parliamentary debates.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Notes should focus on the historical context contemporary with the 1752 document.

answer.text: A generic summary of world geography without mentioning Nova Scotia.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Historical notes must be specific to the text and its historical setting.

answer.text: An assertion that Chief Cope was a fictional character invented by British scribes.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Cope was a well-documented historical leader in colonial records.

name.text: 22 Question: Hands-On Walkthrough: Drafting Intertextual Notes

questiontext.text: In Olyvia's project on Maud Lewis, how does an intertextual note connect her 1967 letter to physical objects in public museums?

generalfeedback.text: Intertextual notes connect primary documents to related legal statutes, personal correspondence, and preserved museum artifacts.

answer.text: It links her written mention of painting 'oxen and cats' to specific surviving folk art compositions preserved in the Art Gallery of Nova Scotia.

feedback.text: Correct. Intertextual notes connect textual references to physical artworks, museum accession numbers, and related primary sources.

answer.text: It claims that Maud Lewis personally built the museum building in Halifax.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Lewis was a folk painter who lived in Digby County; her works were acquired by the museum.

answer.text: It requires the museum to transfer ownership of the paintings to the student editor.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Commentary notes document cultural connections without affecting legal museum property rights.

answer.text: It asserts that cats and oxen were mythical creatures that did not exist in Nova Scotia.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both were standard domestic farm animals frequently depicted in Maritime folk art.

name.text: 23 Question: Validating Pointers and Link Integrity in VS Code

questiontext.text: How can you quickly detect orphaned annotation pointers in Visual Studio Code using search?

generalfeedback.text: Validate link integrity in VS Code by verifying that every `@target` includes the `#` prefix and matches an existing `xml:id`.

answer.text: Search for the anchor target ID using Cmd+F / Ctrl+F and confirm that it matches an exact xml:id declaration elsewhere in the file.

feedback.text: Correct. Every target pointer must match an existing xml:id; finding only one occurrence reveals an orphaned pointer.

answer.text: Restart your computer three times in succession.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Restarting hardware does not audit XML pointer references.

answer.text: Print the XML code onto paper and inspect it with a magnifying glass.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Software search in VS Code is vastly faster and less error-prone than manual paper inspection.

answer.text: Delete all IDs so that no links can ever break.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Deleting IDs destroys the entire annotation linkage architecture.

name.text: 24 Question: Case Study: The Dickinson College Commentaries Model

questiontext.text: What key pedagogical design feature makes the Dickinson College Commentaries model highly effective for student readers?

generalfeedback.text: The Dickinson College Commentaries model shows how clean visual separation, controlled categories, and linked gazetteers make historical texts accessible to students.

answer.text: It cleanly separates base reading text from collapsible commentary sidebars, grouping notes into distinct lexical, grammatical, and historical categories.

feedback.text: Correct. DCC avoids visual clutter by categorizing notes and displaying them in dedicated side panels beside the clean reading text.

answer.text: It translates every historical text into computer binary code.

feedback.text: Incorrect. DCC editions are designed for human students learning historical languages, not computers.

answer.text: It requires students to pass an entrance exam before allowing them to view the website.

feedback.text: Incorrect. DCC is an open-access public humanities project.

answer.text: It deletes all historical names from the text to avoid confusing novices.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Historical names are retained and enriched with gazetteer links.

name.text: 25 Question: Case Study: Scholarly Commentary in Legal and archive Editions

questiontext.text: When annotating official state documents like the 1791 French decree or the 1752 British treaty, why must commentary examine institutional authority?

generalfeedback.text: archive and legal commentary studies legislative standard, historical precedents, and the social realities behind official administrative rhetoric.

answer.text: Because official documents reflect specific legal jurisdictions and political power struggles that determine whether an act had binding legal validity.

feedback.text: Correct. Legal commentary must explain who held legislative power, what royal sanctions were required, and how laws were received by the public.

answer.text: Because legal documents are always works of pure fiction that have no historical consequences.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Treaties and revolutionary decrees had profound political and economic consequences.

answer.text: Because the TEI Guidelines forbid annotating non-legal texts.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI is used for literature, personal letters, religious texts, and archival records alike.

answer.text: Because editors are required to agree with all actions taken by historical governments.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Critical commentary maintains scholarly objectivity and evaluates historical realities.

name.text: 26 Question: Designing Your Commentary Editorial Policy

questiontext.text: What is the primary benefit of defining a written Commentary Editorial Policy in COMMENTARY.md before annotating?

generalfeedback.text: Establish a clear commentary editorial policy defining target audience, entity naming rules, and note length limits before writing.

answer.text: It establishes consistent rules for target audience, entity identification thresholds, and note length limits, preventing uneven coverage across the edition.

feedback.text: Correct. A written policy ensures that all parts of the document receive balanced, consistent scholarly attention.

answer.text: It guarantees that the edition will automatically win international book prizes.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Editorial policies ensure consistency and rigor, but do not guarantee awards.

answer.text: It allows the editor to skip verifying facts in historical dictionaries.

feedback.text: Incorrect. An editorial policy mandates rigorous fact-checking rather than skipping it.

answer.text: It restricts the edition to being read only on Apple computers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI digital editions are platform-independent.

name.text: 27 Question: Hands-On Exercise: Building the Standoff TEI Shell

questiontext.text: In the complete TEI standoff shell, where does the <standOff> container reside relative to the other major structural elements?

generalfeedback.text: The standoff TEI shell provides a robust structure combining the `teiHeader`, base text record ``, and annotations in ``.

answer.text: Directly after the closing </text> tag and immediately before the final closing </TEI> tag.

feedback.text: Correct. The <standOff> element is a direct child of <TEI>, sitting alongside <teiHeader> and <text>.

answer.text: Inside the <teiHeader> within the title statement.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The teiHeader describes document metadata, not standoff annotations.

answer.text: At the very beginning of the file before the XML declaration.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The XML declaration must always be the first line of an XML file.

answer.text: Inside a separate Microsoft Excel spreadsheet file on the Desktop.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The standoff block is an integral part of the TEI XML file.

name.text: 28 Question: Authoring a Five-Note Reference Corpus

questiontext.text: What is the purpose of authoring a diverse five-note manual reference corpus in today's lab milestone?

generalfeedback.text: Authoring five diverse commentary notes creates a reliable manual gold standard for evaluating deterministic search tools and AI models.

answer.text: It establishes a verified, human-curated gold standard across lexical, historical, and intertextual categories for evaluating algorithmic and AI tools later in the week.

feedback.text: Correct. Today's hand-crafted reference notes provide the baseline against which Wednesday's deterministic tools and Friday's AI prompts will be measured.

answer.text: It fulfills the complete publication requirements of a ten-volume academic edition.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Five notes constitute an introductory laboratory sample, not a complete multi-volume edition.

answer.text: It proves that human editors will never be needed in digital humanities again.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The manual corpus demonstrates that human judgment is the essential foundation of quality annotation.

answer.text: It automatically submits the student's final term paper to Moodle.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It is a laboratory reference corpus for comparative benchmarking.

name.text: 29 Question: Documenting Your Manual Notes in COMMENTARY.md

questiontext.text: Why is maintaining a research ledger in COMMENTARY.md a vital practice in digital scholarly editing?

generalfeedback.text: Document your research process and note inventory in `COMMENTARY.md` to maintain a permanent record of your editorial sources and methodology.

answer.text: It records consulted dictionaries, historical sources, note inventories, and reflective analysis, providing a durable audit trail of editorial decisions.

feedback.text: Correct. A documentation ledger tracks the research evidence supporting every note and documents the editor's methodological decisions.

answer.text: It replaces the XML file so that students do not need to learn digital markup.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The markdown ledger documents the XML edition; it does not replace it.

answer.text: It deletes all previous git commit messages from the repository history.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Ledgers document project work and are tracked in git alongside code and markup.

answer.text: It is an optional decorative exercise with no academic or professional value.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Transparent research documentation is a core standard of professional digital scholarship.

name.text: 30 Question: Synthesis: The Human-in-the-Loop Foundation

questiontext.text: What core principle governs the relationship between human scholars and automated digital or AI tools in text commentary?

generalfeedback.text: Manual commentary sets up the irreplaceable human gold standard against which all automated and AI-assisted annotation tools must be evaluated.

answer.text: Automated tools can assist with search and draft generation, but human scholars remain the essential authority responsible for critical judgment and verification.

feedback.text: Correct. The human-in-the-loop principle ensures that technology accelerates editorial workflows while human experts guarantee intellectual integrity.

answer.text: AI models should be allowed to publish commentary without human review or oversight.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Unreviewed AI text frequently contains hallucinations, anachronisms, and fake citations.

answer.text: Human scholars should refuse to use computers or search engines under any circumstances.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Computational tools are powerful aids when guided by trained human judgment.

answer.text: Algorithms always understand historical documents better than human historians.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Language models process statistical token patterns, lacking genuine historical understanding or lived experience.
